## Unix-like systems and bash

### 1. Logging on to the Falcon Supercomputer

Prerequisites

- Consult Falcon documentation from Ade Fewings: https://bangoroffice365.sharepoint.com/sites/DigitalServices/SitePages/The-Falcon-Supercomputer.aspx
- Windows users need to download the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) (other solutions exist)
- Linux and Mac users can just ssh from the terminal

You will interact with four main systems:

- **COGS** – The account portal where you request and manage your Falcon login (username and password).
  - https://cogs.cf.ac.uk
- **ColdFront** – Normally only PIs need to access ColdFront. The portal where projects, project membership, and compute allocations are managed. 
  - https://coldfront.cf.ac.uk
- **Falcon login node** – The HPC login server where you log in and run jobs.
  - `falcon_username@falconlogin.cf.ac.uk`
- **Bangor's SSH Bastion** – The gateway you must connect through before you can reach Falcon.
  - `bangor_username@ssh.bangor.ac.uk`

Important Note: COGS and ColdFront are reachable directly from the Bangor LAN - e.g. campus managed wired, VPN or via standard Bangor remote access solutions such as the Linux Desktop available through eResearch OnDemand. Also note:

- your bangor_username for the ssh server and falcon_username are different
- bangor_username has your normal password with MFA
- falcon_username password (suggest no special characters) can be set in COGS

```bash
# Linux/Mac/WSL
# Open a terminal
ssh you25usr@ssh.bangor.ac.uk
# enter your bangor password and complete MFA

# from bangor ssh server, log into falcon
ssh b.you25usr@falconlogin.cf.ac.uk

# ! advanced option: all-in-one
ssh -J you25usr@ssh.bangor.ac.uk b.you25usr@falconlogin.cf.ac.uk

```

### 2. Basic bash commands

Unix-like (linux and Mac) generally use a bash shell (or something like it).

"*Bash is a command processor that typically runs in a text window where the user types commands that cause actions. Bash can also read and execute commands from a file, called a shell script. Like most Unix shells, it supports filename globbing (wildcard matching), piping, here documents, command substitution, variables, and control structures for condition-testing and iteration.*" 

See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bash_(Unix_shell)

```bash
# print working directory
pwd

# make directory
mkdir my_directory

# change directory
cd my_directory

# print working directory
pwd

# print something to screen
echo "hello"

# redirect output to file 
echo "hello" > hello.txt

# list contents of directory
ls

# help menu
ls --help

# view contents of file
cat
less
head

# print something else to file
echo "hello2" > hello.txt
echo "hello" > hello.txt
echo "hello2" >> hello.txt

# count lines and characters
wc -l
wc -c

# search for content in files
grep --help
grep "2" hello.txt

# pipes
grep "2" hello.txt | wc -l

# deleting (CAREFUL!!!)
rm hello.txt

# let's make some more files
yes hello | head -n 100 > my_file1.txt
yes goodbye | head -n 100 > my_file2.txt

# wildcards
cat my_file* > my_combined_file.txt

# a note on file extensions
mv my_combined_file2.txt my_combined_file2.mp3
mv my_combined_file2.txt my_combined_file2

# deleting with wildcards (VERY CAREFUL!!!)
rm my*

# Download file from internet: e.g. NCBI
wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/964/194/415/GCF_964194415.1_rVipBer3.hap1.1/GCF_964194415.1_rVipBer3.hap1.1_genomic.fna.gz

# Note file is compressed with gzip compression
# view contents without unzipping
zcat GCF_964194415.1_rVipBer3.hap1.1_genomic.fna.gz | less

# uncompress
gunzip GCF_964194415.1_rVipBer3.hap1.1_genomic.fna.gz
# note you can compress with the command gzip

# log off
exit

```

### 4. Bash scripts

- Bash scripts allow sets of commands to be executed in an automated fashion
- Files contain bash scripts are given the extension `.sh` by convention
- fist line is the bash **shebang**, it instructs the system to parse the file using `bash` (as opposed to `python, perl, R`, etc.)
- lines starting `#` are comments
- commands are executed from top to bottom

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# let's make some files
yes hello | head -n 100 > my_file1.txt
yes goodbye | head -n 100 > my_file2.txt

# combine files
cat my_file* > my_combined_file.txt

echo "job finished"
```

#### A note on text editors

- never (ever) use a word processor
- plain text editor (many available)
- includes terminal plain text editors
- be careful windows people :)
- example: `vim`

```bash
# open file
vim my_script.sh

# enter insert mode
i

# do stuff ######################################

# exit insert mode 
[ESC]

# write changes to file
:w

# quit
:q
```

#### Executing bash scripts

```bash
sh my_script.sh
```

### 6. Variables

- In `bash`, variables can be used to store data in memory
- Works exactly like objects in `R`
- After they are defined, variables can be recalled using `$`
- anything entered after the script call becomes variables `$1, $2, $3`, etc. 
- Or they can be defined in the script `variable=value`

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# script makes lists of 2 words, which can be entered when the script is called
# $count controls the length of the list
# call the script like:
# sh my_script.sh hello goodbye

# declare variables
count=100

# main script 

# let's make some files
yes $1 | head -n $count > my_file1.txt
yes $2 | head -n $count > my_file2.txt

# combine files
cat my_file* > my_combined_file.txt

echo "job finished"
```

### 7. Loops

- Loops are quite an advanced feature, but extremely useful
- different types of loop `while`, `for`, `if`, and many more
- here we look at a basic while loop with a counter

```bash
#!/bin/bash 

x=0

while [ $x -lt 10 ]; do
  echo The counter is $x
  let x=x+1
done
```

### 8.`for` loops

- `for` loops are extremely useful for iterating over files in a directory, or over a list of items
- it's a way of doing things automatically and sequentially

```bash

cat are_these_all_adder_scaffolds.txt

```

```bash

# execute a command for each scaffold in the list
for x in $(cat are_these_all_adder_scaffolds.txt); do
  echo $x
done

# the variable can be any word which could help with clarity
for scaffold in $(cat are_these_all_adder_scaffolds.txt); do
  echo $scaffold
done

# you can do multiple commands in the loop, but you need to use `;` to separate them
for scaffold in $(cat are_these_all_adder_scaffolds.txt); do
  echo $scaffold;
  grep -c "$scaffold" GCF_964194415.1_rVipBer3.hap1.1_genomic.fna
done

# other cool loops: if loops
if grep -c "chromosome: 1" GCF_964194415.1_rVipBer3.hap1.1_genomic.fna; then
  echo "did I find a chromosome?"
fi

```

- and they can even be nested!

```bash

for scaffold in $(cat are_these_all_adder_scaffolds.txt); do

  if grep "$scaffold" GCF_964194415.1_rVipBer3.hap1.1_genomic.fna; then
    echo "${scaffold} is present :)"
  fi

done

```

## `markdown` and `Rmarkdown` in `Rstudio`

At this stage, you may be taking notes on commands and results in some way. We suggest `markdown` is the best option for this. It is a simple text format that allows you to combine text, code and results in a single document, and knit to html to view in an internet browser.

`Rmarkdown` is an one implementation of markdown for use within `Rstudio`. An `Rmarkdown` document is written in markdown and contains chunks of embedded `R` code, which can be executed and results knitted to the html.

- In Rstudio select File > New File > R Markdown
- Below is a simple example that we will work though

```bash
# this is an example yaml header that goes at the top of the document
---
title: "R markdown example"
author: "Axel Barlow"
date: "2023-10-31"
output:
  html_document:
    keep_md: true
---
```

The setup chunk is a special code chunk that is executed at the start of the document. It is used to set options for the document and load libraries.

```r
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

### 5. Slurm scripts

- Running a live terminal is not very convenient
- We need a way of submitting jobs to the queue: `slurm` job script
- It's just a bash script, with additional options passed to `slurm` using `#SBATCH` 

```bash
#!/bin/bash --login
###
#job name
#SBATCH --job-name=example
#job stdout file
#SBATCH --output=/path/to/dir/example%J
#job stderr file
#SBATCH --error=/path/to/dir/example_err%J
#maximum job time in D-HH:MM
#SBATCH --time=0-00:01
#number of nodes
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#number of parallel processes (tasks)
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#memory in Gb 
#SBATCH --mem=1G
#specify project
#SBATCH --account SCWF00251_j_paijmans_246

echo hello > hello.txt
```

```bash
# submit to queue
sbatch job_script.sh
```

## Population genomics: genotype likelihoods and population structure

Our shared project directory is `/scratch/SCWF00251/`

### 1. Tour and `BEARCAVE`

```bash
# enter project directory
cd /scratch/SCWF00251/

# view directories
ll

# bams
cd BEARCAVE2/mappedrVipBer3_chr6/
ll

# ref genome
ll ../refgenomes/rVipBer3_chr6/

# look at coverage
module load SAMtools
samtools tview adder0X_XXX_chr6.bam ../refgenomes/rVipBer3_chr6/rVipBer3_chr6.fa
samtools coverage adder0X_XXX_chr6.bam | head -2
```

### 2. Compute genotype likelihoods in `angsd`

We will compute genotype likelihoods using `angsd`. This requires a list of bamfiles (with full paths) to analyse. For example:

```bash
# angsd requires a list of bam files in a text file
ls -1 /scratch/SCWF00251/BEARCAVE2/mappedrVipBer3_chr6/*bam > bamlist_all.txt
```

For `angsd` documentation see: https://github.com/angsd/angsd

```bash
# load angsd module
module purge
module load angsd/0.940-GCC-12.3.0

# angsd command
#-b = specify bamlist
#-GL = specify genotype likelihood model
#-doMajorMinor = identify major/minor allele using genotype likelihoods
#-doGlf = output genotype likelihoods in beagle format
#-doMaf = calculate minor allele frequency
#-SNP_pval = p-value for SNP calling
#-minMapQ = minimum mapping quality
#-minQ = minimum base quality
#-minMaf = minimum minor allele frequency
#-minInd = minimum number of individuals with data
#-setMinDepthInd = minimum depth per individual
#-doCounts = count number of sampled alleles (required for -seMinDepthInd)
#-out = output file prefix
#-nThreads = number of threads to use

# this calculates the genotype likelihoods for all samples in the bamlist and outputs as a beagle file
angsd -b bamlist_all.txt -GL 1 -doMajorMinor 1 -doGlf 2 -doMaf 1 -SNP_pval 1e-6 -minMapQ 30 -minQ 30 -minMaf 0.1 -minInd 50 -setMinDepthInd 4 -doCounts 1 -out all_gl -nThreads 6
```


### 4. Allele covariance matrix using `PCangsd`

We will use the beagle file generated by `angsd` to compute an allele covariance matrix using `PCangsd`. This is a fast and efficient way to compute PCA from genotype likelihoods.

See: https://github.com/rosemeis/pcangsd

```bash
module purge
module load PCAngsd/1.36.4-gfbf-2025a

#--beagle = specify beagle file
#--eig = number of eigenvectors to compute
#--threads = number of threads to use
#--out = output file prefix

# run PCangsd
pcangsd --beagle all_gl.beagle.gz --eig 2 --threads 4 --out all_gl_pcangsd
```

### 5. Genetic distance matrix using `ngsDist`

We will use the beagle file generated by `angsd` to compute a genetic distance matrix using `ngsDist`. This is a fast and efficient way to compute genetic distances from genotype likelihoods.

See: https://github.com/fgvieira/ngsDist

```bash
module purge
module load ngsDist/1.0.10-foss-2025a

#--geno all_gl.beagle.gz = specify beagle file
#--probs = input is genotype likelihoods
#--n_ind = number of individuals
#--n_sites = number of sites [note you need to find this out!]
#--posH = specify mafs file [H indicates header]
#--out = output file prefix
#--n_threads = number of threads to use

# run ngsDist
ngsDist --geno all_gl.beagle.gz --probs --n_ind 50 --n_sites XXXXX --posH all_gl.mafs --out all_gl_dist.mat --n_threads 4
```

### 6. `STRUCTURE`-type analysis using `ngsAdmix`

We will use the beagle file generated by `angsd` to compute a STRUCTURE analysis using `ngsAdmix`. This is a fast and efficient way to assign individuals to K populations and to compute admixture proportions from genotype likelihoods.

See: https://github.com/aalbrechtsen/NGSadmix

```bash
module purge
module load angsd/0.940-GCC-12.3.0

#-likes = specify beagle file
#-K = number of populations
#-P = number of threads to use
#-outfiles = output file prefix

# run ngsAdmix, included in angsd module
NGSadmix -likes all_gl.beagle.gz -K 5 -P 4 -outfiles all_gl_admix_k5
```

### 1. PCA

```{r, out.width = "50%", fig.align = "center", fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 5}
# read in covariance matrix
my_cov <- as.matrix(read.table("./assets/data/all_gl_pcangsd.cov"))

# read in adder info
adders <- read.table("./assets/data/adder_info_2026.txt", header=T, sep=',')

# do PCA
my_pca <- eigen(my_cov)
# the output is a list with two parts:
# $values = vector of eigen values 
# $vectors = matrix of eigen vectors

# look at eigen values
my_pca$values

# plot
# colours are just a vector of colours, one for each sample, in order of bamlist
plot(my_pca$vectors[,1], my_pca$vectors[,2],
     pch=21, bg=adders$col
)
```

## Population genomics: genetic diversity

### 1. Heterozygosity

Our estimate of heterozygosity is the SFS for a single individual in sliding windows across chromosome 6. This requires a single bam file (with full path) to analyse and an outgroup, for which we will used the related species *Vipera ursinii*. `angsd` is used to first calculate GLs and allele frequencies. `realSFS` which is included in `angsd` is then used to compute the SFS.

```bash
# set files as variables
input='/scratch/SCWF00251/BEARCAVE2/mappedrVipBer3_chr6/adderXX_YYY_chr6.bam'
output='adderXX_het'
# We need to specify the ancestral allele, use fasta generated from Vipera ursinii outgroup
urs='/scratch/SCWF00251/BEARCAVE2/outgroups/ursinii01_rom_chr6.fa'

# depth variables
min=4

# estimate genotype likelihoods
# -i = input file
# -doSaf = per-site allele frequencies
# -GL = genotype likelihood model
# -P = number threads
# -anc = outgroup, to identify ancestral allele
# -minQ,-minMapQ = min base and map quality
# -setMinDepthInd = min depth filter
angsd -i $input -doSaf 1 -GL 1 -P 4 -anc $urs -out $output -minMapQ 30 -minQ 30 -setMinDepthInd $min -doCounts 1

# calculate sfs
# -nSites = sliding window size
# -P = no threads
realSFS $output.saf.idx -nSites 50000 -P 4 > $output.window.sfs
```

### 2. Population genetic diversity

We require a list of bamfiles (with full paths) from a single population to analyse. For example:

```bash
# angsd requires a list of bam files from one population in a text file
ls -1 /scratch/SCWF00251/BEARCAVE2/mappedrVipBer3_chr6/*bam | grep ang > bamlist_ang.txt
```

Next we will compute various population genetic diversity metrics in sliding windows across chromosome 6. We first compute GLs and allele frequencies in `angsd`, then use `realSFS` for the SFS, and finally `thetastat` for the diversity metrics in a sliding window.

```bash
# set files as variables
# We need to specify the ancestral allele, use fasta generated from Vipera ursinii outgroup
urs='/scratch/SCWF00251/BEARCAVE2/outgroups/ursinii01_rom_chr6.fa'
outpop='ang'

# depth variables
min=4

# estimate genotype likelihoods
# -b = input bam list
# -doSaf = per-site allele frequencies
# -GL = genotype likelihood model
# -P = number threads
# -anc = outgroup, to identify ancestral allele
# -minQ,-minMapQ = min base and map quality
# -setMinDepthInd = min depth filter
# -minInd = minimum number of individuals with data
angsd -b bamlist_ang.txt -doSaf 1 -doMaf 1 -GL 1 -P 4 -doMajorMinor 1 -anc $urs -out $outpop -minMapQ 30 -minQ 30 -setMinDepthInd 4 -minInd 7 -doCounts 1

#get 1d sfs for population
realSFS $outpop.saf.idx -P 4 > $outpop.sfs

#combine saf and sfs to generate per site theta values
realSFS saf2theta $outpop.saf.idx -sfs $outpop.sfs -outname $outpop

#make slidingwindow files from it
thetaStat do_stat $outpop.thetas.idx -win 50000 -step 50000 -outnames $output.50kb.thetas.txt
```

## Phylogenomics

We will change datasets for phylogenomics. We have datasets from 7 species of European viper mapped to chromosome 6. The mapping reference is *Macrovipera schweizeri*, which is an outgroup. This avoids any issues with mapping reference bias. 

Bam files are located in `/scratch/SCWF00251/BEARCAVE2/mappedrMacScw_chr6/`. 

```bash
ls -1 *bam

ammodytes_chr6.bam
aspis_chr6.bam
berus_UK_chr6.bam
latastei_chr6.bam
seoani_chr6.bam
ursinii_chr6.bam
```

The reference genome is: `/scratch/SCWF00251/BEARCAVE2/refgenomes/rMacScw_chr6/rMacScw1_chr6.fa`.

### 1. Consensus fasta

We use `angsd` to generate a consensus fasta using the `-doFasta` command

```bash
#-doFasta 2 = generate consensus fasta using the most frequent base
#-minQ -minMapQ = minimum base and map quality
#-setMinDepthInd = minimum depth
#-basesPerLine = number of bases per line in output fasta, set to > chromosome size [believe me you will thank me for this later]
angsd -doFasta 2 -doCounts 1 -minQ 30 -minMapQ 30 -setMinDepthInd 3 -basesPerLine 100000000 -i /scratch/SCWF00251/BEARCAVE2/mappedrMacScw_chr6/ammodytes_chr6.bam -out ammodytes_chr6
```

- Johanna live coding hackathon

Once you have an alignment, we can strip out invariant sites and sites with missing data using `snp-sites`. 

```bash
module load snp-sites/2.5.1-GCCcore-12.3.0

# run snp-sites
# -c = remove sites with missing data
snp-sites -c alignment_file.fa > alignment_chr6.fa
```

### 3. Maximum likelihood analysis using `iqtree`

```bash
module purge
module load IQ-TREE/3.0.1-gompi-2024a

# run iqtree
# -s = input alignment
# -o = outgroup
# -T = number of threads
# -B = number of bootstrap replicates
# -m GTR+ASC = GTR model of sequence evolution for ascertained SNPs
# --redo = overwrite existing output files
iqtree3 -s alignment_chr6.fa -o macrovipera_chr6 -T 4 -B 1000 -m GTR+G+ASC --redo
```

### 5. D statistics

We need a bamlist of the 6 *Vipera* species to compute D statistics. We use the reference genome file for the outgroup *Macrovipera schweizeri*.

```bash
# -doAbbababa 1 = compute D statistics using single read sampling
# -minQ -minMapQ = minimum base and map quality
# -b = input bam list
# -anc = outgroup reference genome
# -out = output file prefix
angsd -doAbbababa 1 -doCounts 1 -minQ 30 -minMapQ 30 -b bamlist_phylo -anc /scratch/SCWF00251/BEARCAVE2/refgenomes/rMacScw1_chr6/rMacScw1_chr6.fa -out vipera_dstat -nThreads 4
```

We then carry out the jackknife analysis in `R`

```r
# create a file containing the list of individuals in the order they appear in the bamlist_phylo file
ammodytes_chr6
aspis_chr6
berus_UK_chr6
latastei_chr6
seoani_chr6
ursinii_chr6

# run jackknife with the jackKnife.R script (comes with angsd)
Rscript jackKnife.R file=vipera_dstat.abbababa indNames=indnames_dstat outfile=vipera_dstat_jackknife
```
